extracted.intended_audience: math students, math teachers, and general mathematically-curious readers (math educators/enthusiasts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging and choosing mathematical proofs (short clever 'ditties' vs long standard proofs), emphasizing pedagogical tradeoffs, rigor, elegance, and applicability. Uses concrete examples (e.g., sqrt(2), Euler's identity) to illustrate criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and depth
rubrics_metrics.description: In the somber mood of scholarship ... we prize rigor and depth. The “standard proofs” are standard for good reason. They convey unambiguous truths through careful logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proofs 'stand the test of time' and are preferred when the goal is airtight justification and long-term reliability. Use these when the audience values formal completeness and minimal hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / clever shortcuts (the 'ditty')
rubrics_metrics.description: A nifty shortcut, persuasive but not explanatory — 'sneaky like a thief.' Ditties are fun, provocative, and often far shorter than standard proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good when you want a quick persuasive argument or to spark interest; beware that such proofs may hide assumptions or use techniques that feel like 'black magic' (e.g., separation of variables without ODE background). They may not provide full explanation or be appropriate for formal presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power / insight
rubrics_metrics.description: An elaborate work of architecture — it explains but perhaps overwhelms. If an argument is a connector between one idea and another, explanatory proofs show the mechanism linking concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose these proofs when teaching understanding, general principles, or when you want students to see how results arise from deeper structure. They may be longer but yield transferable insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heavy machinery / reliance on nontrivial results
rubrics_metrics.description: Some short proofs rely on nontrivial results (e.g., Dan’s Ditty relies on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic), which may themselves be advanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about prerequisite results. Avoid using advanced theorems when presenting to audiences who haven't seen them; otherwise the proof risks being circular or pedagogically inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical suitability / audience awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: What do we want from a proof? I say it depends on the spirit in the room. Different moods and audiences (e.g., 14-year-olds vs. scholars) demand different kinds of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match proof choice to students' background and course coverage (e.g., avoid Taylor-series proofs when students haven't seen Taylor series). Consider mood: playful demonstrations vs. solemn rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality and ability to generalize
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs generalize nicely (Dan’s Ditty generalizes to nth roots); others are more specialized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs that suggest generalizations when the goal is to teach broader concepts or to connect to further problems. Note whether the method scales (e.g., to sqrt(3) or nth roots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic value / elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical aesthetics: elegance, concision, and surprising connections (e.g., Euler’s identity linking fundamental constants) are prized features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic appeal can motivate learners and mathematicians; however, elegance should not be confused with completeness. Use elegance to engage, but ensure formal correctness when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation / engagement / playfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ditties are fun. They provoke. They refresh. Presenting contrasting proofs is a great conversation starter and can engage younger or less-engaged students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use playful or surprising proofs to spark interest and motivate deeper inquiry, especially when trying to broaden participation or break monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of definitions and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some arguments 'sweep under the rug' how objects are defined (e.g., how e^{it} is defined, or extending real operations to complex numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about definitions (domain, function definitions, what operations are permitted). Where complex extensions or new definitions are used, state and justify them to avoid misleading the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of circularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for circular arguments (e.g., using a deep theorem that itself depends on the fact you're trying to prove).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the proof's dependencies do not implicitly assume the conclusion. Example: a purported proof of irrationality that uses a theorem whose proof uses irrationality would be circular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of manipulations / analytic cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain manipulations require justification (e.g., rearranging terms of infinite series needs absolute convergence; solving ODEs by separation of variables must be justified via chain rule or uniqueness theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify technical conditions (convergence, differentiability, validity of substituting complex values into series) before using manipulations; when teaching, either justify them or note the gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasiveness versus formal proof status
rubrics_metrics.description: Some arguments function as 'reasons to believe' rather than fully rigorous proofs; they are persuasive but may not meet formal proof standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label such arguments appropriately (heuristic, sketch, motivation) and follow with a rigorous argument when formal proof is required. Use multiple complementary arguments to build conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of active learning and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Good proofs can prompt follow-up questions/exercises (e.g., 'Can you use this method to prove sqrt(3) is irrational?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select proofs that lead naturally to student exercises and checks of understanding. Use simpler or more intuitive proofs to scaffold attempts at generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual appropriateness (spirit of the room)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's repeated phrase: 'it depends on the spirit in the room' — the same result may call for different proofs depending on context and occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the moment calls for a quick demonstration, a deep classroom exploration, a formal write-up, or an aesthetic aside. Tailor level of detail and formality accordingly.
